messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Chaplain
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Crowding: Crowded places, Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Vinh's Reckoning

Vinh Pham was thirty-four when the two men took his wallet on a Tuesday evening in March, but it was not the loss of money that had unmade him. He had been walking home from the hospital chaplaincy office in downtown Portland, cutting through the parking garage as he had done hundreds of times before, when he heard the footsteps accelerate behind him. The first punch came without warning. He remembered the sound of his own breathing—rapid, panicked—and then theirs, the heavy, controlled breathing of men who had done this before. One of them smelled like cigarettes and something sweet, maybe cologne or cheap aftershave, a scent that had burned itself into his nervous system with the force of a brand.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. Two cracked ribs, a split lip, bruising across his left shoulder. But something else had fractured in that garage, something that had not mended. Vinh had come to believe, in the months that followed, that the attack had happened precisely because of who he was. He was too trusting, too naive, the kind of man who walked alone through parking garages in the evening without sufficient wariness. Someone else—someone more careful, more streetwise, more fundamentally capable—would have seen the danger and avoided it. He was certain that his fundamental character had made him a target, had marked him as prey. And if his own nature could betray him so completely in a parking garage, what could stop it from doing so again?

The triggers had accumulated like sediment. Crowded places became impossible. The hospital chaplaincy had always demanded that Vinh move through hallways, waiting rooms, and emergency departments filled with people, but now each crowd felt like a gauntlet of potential threats. He began arriving earlier, leaving later, timing his movements to avoid the busiest hours. Then he started taking routes that avoided the main corridors entirely. His colleagues noticed he was less available, that his presence on the floors had diminished. Within four months, his supervisor had gently suggested that perhaps Vinh might benefit from reassignment to administrative chaplaincy work, something less demanding. The implication was clear: he was no longer reliable in his primary role.

But it was not simply crowds. Specific people triggered the memories with photographic clarity—the images would flash without warning, vivid and unbidden. He would see a man with the same build as one of his attackers, or catch a glimpse of someone with similar features, and the garage would materialize around him again. The visual memories were so precise, so intrusive, that he had begun to avoid places where he might encounter strangers who resembled them. He stopped going to the grocery store at certain times. He declined social invitations to restaurants and gatherings.

The worst part was the rage. When the memories surfaced—the images, the smell, the feeling of helplessness—a fury would ignite in his chest so intense that it frightened him. He was not an angry man by nature; his work as a chaplain had taught him patience and compassion. But now, sitting alone in his apartment at night, he would find himself trembling with rage at the men, at himself, at a world that had revealed itself to be far more dangerous than he had ever understood. He had no power to stop bad things from happening. The attack had proven that. He was vulnerable in ways he could not control, and that knowledge sat in his chest like a stone.

Vinh's wife, Michelle, had died of cancer two years before the mugging. He had learned something about grief then, about the long work of carrying loss. But this was different. This was not the ache of absence; it was the presence of threat, the knowledge that he could be harmed and could do nothing to prevent it. After six months of declining work performance and increasing isolation, Vinh finally made an appointment with a trauma specialist. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the possibility that he would never feel safe again, that the man he had been before the garage—the man who could walk through the world with quiet confidence—was gone forever.
